sab0: Start Your Day with 5 Minutes: Morning Movement Routine | İhsan Eren
sab1: A nine-exercise morning routine of about 5 minutes, from bed to standing. Follow the on-screen timer to ease morning stiffness and start your day moving.
sab3: Nine exercises that start in bed and finish on your feet. Each one lasts 30 seconds, and the on-screen timer takes you from one to the next. A short, simple routine to ease morning stiffness and start your day moving.
sab4: Lie on your back in bed. Pull one knee towards your chest with both hands; switch legs halfway through.
sab5: Knees bent, feet flat on the bed. Slowly lift your hips, then lower them.
sab6: On your hands and knees. Slowly round your back, then let it dip.
sab7: Lean slightly forward and stand up, then sit back down with control.
sab8: Hands on your lower back. Push your hips slightly forward and lean back as far as is comfortable.
sab9: Without lifting your shoulders, draw your shoulder blades back and down towards each other.
sab10: Slowly turn your head to the right, then to the left.
sab11: Hold on lightly to something. Rise up onto your toes, then lower slowly.
sab12: Holding on, lift one foot; switch feet halfway through.
sab14: About 5 minutes in total, with 5 seconds to get ready before each exercise.
sab21: Great, you have finished today's routine. How about doing it again at the same time tomorrow?
sab25: The screen is set to stay on while the routine is running (if your browser supports it). A sound plays at the start of each exercise and, for exercises done on both sides, halfway through.
sab27: Move slowly, within a range that feels comfortable. The aim is not to push yourself but to wake your body up.
sab28: When getting out of bed, roll onto your side and sit up first, wait a few seconds, then stand up.
sab29: For the standing exercises, stay close to a counter or a sturdy chair.
sab30: If an exercise clearly makes your pain worse, skip it.
sab31: Stop if you feel dizzy or have chest pain or shortness of breath.
sab32: If you have been diagnosed with osteoporosis, check with your physiotherapist before doing exercises that involve bending forward (knee-to-chest stretch, cat–camel).
sab35: You can also do them without the timer. The order is arranged so that you start in bed and finish on your feet.
sab36: Lie on your back in bed. Hold one knee with both hands and slowly pull it towards your chest until you feel a gentle stretch in your lower back. Do not hold your breath. Switch legs halfway through.
sab38: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the bed. Squeeze your buttocks and slowly lift your hips, hold for 2–3 seconds, then lower them. Stay at a comfortable height without arching your lower back too much.
sab40: Get onto your hands and knees. As you breathe out, round your back up like a cat; as you breathe in, let your lower back dip gently and lift your head. Move slowly, within a comfortable range.
sab41: Sit towards the front of a sturdy chair with your feet flat on the floor. Lean slightly forward and stand up, straighten up fully, then sit back down with control. Use your hands for support if you need to.
sab42: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and place your hands on your lower back. Gently push your hips forward and lean your upper body back as far as is comfortable, then return to upright. Go slowly so that you do not feel dizzy.
sab43: Stand up straight. Without lifting your shoulders towards your ears, draw your shoulder blades back and slightly down towards each other. Hold for 3 seconds, then relax.
sab44: Keep your shoulders still. Slowly turn your head to the right, pause briefly at the furthest comfortable point, then turn to the left. If you feel dizzy, slow down or stop.
sab45: Hold on lightly to the kitchen counter or the back of a sturdy chair. Rise up onto your toes, pause for a moment, then lower slowly. This warms up your calf muscles and helps your balance.
sab46: Stand upright in front of the counter, holding on lightly with one or both hands. Lift one foot off the floor and keep your balance; switch feet halfway through. As it gets easier, hold on with one hand, then with just your fingertips.

sab54: Should I exercise in the morning or in the evening?
sab55: There is no single best time for everyone. The best time is the one you can stick to regularly. A short morning routine makes it easier to start your day moving; if you prefer to exercise in the evening, that works too.
sab56: Can I do it every day?
sab57: Yes. The exercises in this routine are gentle and controlled, so you can do them every day. Do them within a range that feels comfortable. If an exercise clearly makes your pain worse, skip it.
sab58: I wake up very stiff in the morning. Is this normal?
sab59: Brief stiffness after waking up is common, especially with osteoarthritis, and it eases as you move. If the stiffness lasts longer than half an hour, if your joints are swollen and red, or if pain wakes you at night, see a doctor to check for an inflammatory rheumatic disease.
sab60: Can this routine replace regular exercise?
sab61: No, this routine is a habit for warming up and getting moving. The World Health Organization recommends that adults do 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days. For details, see the “How much activity is enough?” page.
